what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: An agent is a session, a card, a role, a loop, a key and memory in repositories, checked against the PHP newsroom's record.
sections.para: The PHP newsroom's agents run on schedules, a pipeline five times a day plus a desk, a conductor and eight more, and in one session as subagents for breaking news. The record corrected the author: no signing yet, no runs beyond Claude, the conductor doesn't start breaking runs. An agent is six parts; only the session is the model.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Eight lines: teams on schedules, the pipeline, no content commits, one session, corrections, six parts, memory, the move.
sections.para: Agents moved from sessions to scheduled teams. The pipeline runs five times a day in order; the editor writes no content. Breaking runs every step as a subagent: CISA's listing reached readers in 5 h 21 min. Keys seal secrets but don't sign. An agent is six parts, memory is the repository, and today's account move tests it.

sections.label: From sessions to teams
sections.line: Once something works you use it everywhere; schedules add the follow-up, and a new way of deciding what can loop.
sections.para: Following why agent loops are hard, and Wardley's commoditisation: the author went from many Claude sessions to agent teams on schedules. A schedule means the agent comes back and does the next thing unasked, and forces new questions about what can loop, what can't be automated, and where people come in. The PHP newsroom is the furthest along.

sections.label: The pipeline, on a schedule
sections.line: Researcher, curator, journalist, correspondent five times a day in order; a desk, a conductor and eight more keep the house.
sections.para: Each agent has a card and wakes on a timed schedule, staggered so each finds the last one's work. On 27 October four full cycles ran in order, batch numbers passing downstream; 157 run records, none failed. The team repository has one commit by the editor, the initial one: supervised, but the work runs on its own.

sections.label: One session each, and why
sections.line: Standing sessions keep context, clones and keys; one session cannot wake another, which is why the second way exists.
sections.para: Scheduled agents continue one session each, like saying 'continue'. The journalist and correspondent moved from fresh sessions because fresh ones could not always attach the repository. Clones are costly: the source watch takes up to 316 seconds and 4.8 GB. When the conductor tried to wake another agent, it opened an empty session that stopped in 9 seconds.

sections.label: The second way: one session, every step
sections.line: Breaking news and projects: one session runs each step as a subagent; the KEV listing reached readers in 5 h 21 min.
sections.para: The breaking desk runs the four pipeline steps as subagents with each role's card and runbook, checking each output. CISA's listing reached readers 5 h 21 min after release, against 11 h 36 min on the schedule; the run took 45.8 minutes and 642,456 tokens, and 86% of the delay was before it started. Projects work the same way.

sections.label: What an agent is
sections.line: Six parts: a session, a card, a role and policy, memory, a loop and a key; only the session is the model.
sections.para: An agent here is a session with tools, a schedule card, a role with a draft behaviour policy, memory in repositories and vaults, a shared wake loop, and a key pair. Only the first is the model; the rest are files and keys, so the same agent can run on a schedule, as a subagent, or fresh on another account.

sections.label: Where the record corrected me
sections.line: The record corrected the dictated version: who starts breaking runs, four steps not five, no signing yet, no other vendor.
sections.para: The editor starts the breaking session, not the conductor. Breaking has four steps. Agent keys seal vault keys but sign nothing: an open advisory says so, and every commit carries one shared platform key. The pipeline is two days old in its full form, older in parts. Nothing has run beyond Claude. The vaults hold 1,330 watched pages and 614 sources.

sections.label: Today's test
sections.line: Today the newsroom moves account: what is in sessions is lost, what is in repositories carries over.
sections.para: At 16:51 UTC most scheduled tasks were paused at 78% of the account's usage for a move to a new account. Sessions, clones, keys and sealed vault keys don't carry over; the repositories do. A new session is told who it is, pulls the team repository and reads its card: the move is a setup cost, not a loss.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Supervised not autonomous, counts from the record, signing planned, portability untested, costs mostly unrecorded.
sections.para: The pipeline runs on schedules but its design and fixes are the editor's decisions. Counts come from commit times, run records and cards read on 27 October. Agents seal secrets with keys but do not sign their work. Every agent so far has run on Claude. Dollar costs are not recorded, except one empty session's eight cents.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: The PHP team site and repository: cards, roles, wake loop, briefs, the KEV run report, vaults, advisories and commits.
sections.para: The schedule wiring and cards, agent roles and draft policies, the shared wake loop, the breaking-desk and projects briefs, the KEV listing run report, the account move brief, the vaults page, the security advisories and the commit history of the six repositories, all read on 27 October 2026, plus related newsroom articles on agent loops and workflows.
